column4: Understand user intent and expected outcome
column5: A traveler asks for a cheap weekend return flight to Toronto next month. The agent understands the destination, flexible travel window, and price preference before searching.
column6: You want a weekend away, but you haven't picked the dates. You tell the agent, ‘Find me a cheap return flight to Toronto next month.’ It understands that Toronto is fixed, the weekend is flexible, and price matters most. It searches across weekends instead of assuming you already have exact dates in mind.

column4: Understand user intent and expected outcome
column5: A blind user exploring neighborhood photos says that parks and public transport matter most. The assistant focuses its description on those features instead of describing every visible detail.
column6: You're exploring neighborhood photos before deciding where to live. You tell the assistant, ‘Parks and public transport matter most to me.’ Instead of describing every building and parked car, it focuses on green spaces and visible public transport features. Its description follows what you want to learn about the neighborhood.

column5: A user supplies a blender receipt and warranty-claim instructions. The agent identifies the serial number and fault description as missing, while recognizing that the purchase date is already available.
column6: Your blender has stopped working. You give the agent your receipt and the warranty-claim instructions. It checks what the claim requires against what you've supplied. ‘I have the purchase date,’ it says. ‘I still need the blender's serial number and a description of the fault.’ You know exactly what's missing.

column5: A blind user asks when a reply to a photographed utility notice is due. The assistant notices that the section beginning “Reply by” is cut off and explains that it needs the bottom of the page.
column6: You photograph a utility notice and ask, ‘When do I need to reply?’ The assistant finds the words ‘Reply by,’ but the photograph cuts off before the deadline. It says, ‘The date is outside this photo. Please photograph the bottom of the page.’ It identifies the missing part instead of guessing the answer.

column5: A user asks the agent to match slide two’s background to the title card on slide one. The agent identifies the background color of title is white and uses it for the second slide.
column6: You're editing a presentation and want the slides to look consistent. You say, ‘Make slide two's background match the title card on slide one.’ The agent examines the title card, recognizes that its background is white, and applies white to slide two. You don't have to identify the color or look up its settings yourself.

column5: A blind viewer asks what a person in a paused video is carrying. The assistant examines that moment and describes the object, such as a blue folder held against the person’s chest.
column6: You pause a video because the soundtrack doesn't explain what someone is carrying. You ask the assistant, ‘What's that person holding?’ It examines the paused moment and says, ‘They're holding a blue folder against their chest.’ You get the specific visual detail you asked about, without a description of the entire scene.

column5: A shopper asks for a drink’s dietary details and current offer. The agent gathers the relevant label information and price offer into one response with links to their sources.
column6: You're deciding whether to buy a drink and ask, ‘What are its dietary details, and is there an offer on it?’ The agent gathers the label information and the current price offer. It brings both into one response, with links to where it found them, so you don't have to search separate pages yourself.

column5: Before visiting a library, a low-vision user asks how to recognize its entrance. The agent combines the library’s name and map location with doorway details visible in a street photo.
column6: You're planning a library visit and want to recognize the entrance when you arrive. You ask the agent for help. It brings together the library's name, its location on the map, and doorway details from a street photo. You get a description of where to look and what identifies the entrance, rather than just an address.

column5: A shopper asks for the cheapest sparkling water. Several flavors share the lowest price, so the agent names the options and asks which flavor to choose before adding anything.
column6: You're ordering groceries and say, ‘Add the cheapest sparkling water.’ The agent finds several flavors at the same lowest price. Rather than choosing a flavor for you, it names the tied options and asks, ‘Which flavor would you like?’ It waits for your answer before adding anything to the basket.

column5: A blind user uploads a two-page letter and asks for the important part. The agent asks whether they want the payment details, required action, or whole letter before deciding what to read.
column6: You upload a two-page letter and ask the agent to read the important part. But ‘important’ could mean several things. Before choosing a passage, it asks, ‘Would you like the payment details, what you need to do, or the whole letter?’ Your answer determines what it reads to you.

column5: The agent finds two news reports about the same event the user is asking for. The agent compares the facts both mention and the details each emphasizes, linking its comparison to the original articles.
column6: You want to understand an event in the news and ask the agent to compare two reports. It separates the facts both articles mention from the details each emphasizes. It explains where their accounts overlap and where their focus differs, with links to both articles so you can explore the comparison yourself.

column5: The blind user asks the agent to find a recent email from wholefoods. The agent compares two approaches that can achieves the same goal: one is to directly summarize and read it out to the user, and the other is to operate the computer to locate the email for the user to read and explore by themselves. The agent compares the two approaches and decide which one is better give the user's other needs (e.g., they need the receipt ASAP)
column6: You need information from a recent Whole Foods receipt email right away. The agent weighs two options: read you a summary now, or open the email for you to explore with your screen reader. Because you've said speed matters, it chooses the summary. It selects between two routes to the same information based on your immediate need.

column5: A user asks the agent to close a frozen browser. The agent chooses the browser’s End task command in the process manager because the ordinary close control is not responding.
column6: Your browser has frozen, and its usual close button isn't responding. You ask the agent to close it. Recognizing that another click on the same button won't help, it selects the browser in the process manager and uses ‘End task.’ It chooses an action suited to the problem you're facing.

column5: A low-vision viewer says the video captions are too small. The agent chooses to enlarge the caption text, then leaves the viewer able to judge whether it is readable.
column6: You're watching a video, but the captions are too small to read comfortably. You tell the agent, ‘I can't read the captions.’ It chooses to enlarge the caption text and changes that setting. The video remains available for you to check whether the larger captions now work for you.

column4: Plan out a sequence of steps
column5: A student shares a syllabus and available study times with agent to come up with a study plan. The agent decided to decompose this task into subtasks including: extracting all learning activities needed, figuring our the depdency relationship between different activities, placing foundational activities before dependent ones and optimizing the time for each activity so it's more practical and prevent burning out.
column6: You share your syllabus and available study times, then ask for a study plan. Before building the schedule, the agent breaks its work into steps: list the learning activities, identify which depend on others, put the foundations first, and allow manageable time for each. It plans how to create a schedule that won't overload you.

column4: Plan out a sequence of steps
column5: A blind user shares a scanned (inaccessible) club-registration form. Before entering anything, the agent proposes reading the required fields, gathering answers, preparing a digital copy, and reviewing it together.
column6: You need to join a club, but its scanned registration form doesn't work with your screen reader. You ask the agent to help. Before entering anything, it proposes a sequence: read the required fields, collect your answers, prepare a digital copy, and review it together. You know the route through the task before it begins.

column5: An agent preparing a report cannot extract a scanned table as text. It changes approach by examining the page image, then uses the recovered table information to continue the report.
column6: You ask the agent to prepare a report using a scanned table. Its first attempt to extract the table as text fails. Instead of stopping or repeating the same attempt, it examines the page as an image. It recovers the table's information that way and continues preparing your report.

column5: A low-vision user tries to identify a can, but glare obscures its label. The assistant proposes barcode recognition as an alternative and guides the user to find the barcode.
column6: You're trying to identify a can, but glare across the label makes the photo unreadable. The assistant explains why the label isn't helping and suggests another route: checking the barcode. It guides you to locate the barcode on the can, giving you a different way to identify it when the first approach fails.

column5: While an agent prepares a flight search, the user corrects the departure city. The agent updates the remaining search steps to use the corrected city.
column6: The agent is preparing a flight search when you realize you gave it the wrong departure city. You correct yourself before it finishes. The agent takes in the change and revises the remaining search steps to use the new city. Its work follows your correction instead of continuing with the original plan.

column5: A blind viewer says the video descriptions are too brief. The agent changes its description style to include more about actions, objects, and spatial relationships.
column6: You're listening to a video's audio descriptions, but they leave you unsure what's happening. You tell the agent, ‘These are too brief. I need more detail.’ It adjusts the descriptions that follow to explain more about people's actions, the objects involved, and where things are in relation to each other.

column5: A user asks the agent to combine twelve documents into one PDF. The agent tracks completed and pending documents and reports that nine are processed and three remain.
column6: You ask the agent to combine twelve documents into one PDF. While it works, you want to know how far it's got. The agent keeps track of which documents are finished and which are still waiting. It reports, ‘Nine documents are processed. Three remain.’ You can tell what's done without checking each file yourself.

column5: A blind user completing a scanned housing form togethger with AI. They ask how much is left. The agent identifies the completed sections and reports two unanswered questions and the remaining signature.
column6: You're working through a scanned housing form with the agent and ask, ‘How much is left?’ It checks the sections you've already completed together against those still unfinished. It tells you that two questions still need answers and the signature remains, so you know exactly what's between you and a completed form.

column4: Check whether the outcome is right
column5: After entering a user’s details in a form, the agent compares the visible entries with the original request and flags a mismatch before submission.
column6: You ask the agent to enter your details into a form. Before submitting it, the agent reads back the visible entries and compares them with your original instructions. It spots an entry that doesn't match and flags it for correction. Filling the fields isn't enough; it checks that the result is right.

column4: Check whether the outcome is right
column5: A blind user asks the agent to crop a group photo without excluding anyone. The agent compares the cropped result with the original and flags when a person at the edge has been cut off.
column6: You ask the agent to crop a group photo, with one condition: keep everyone in the picture. After cropping, it compares the result with the original. It notices that a person at the edge has been cut off and flags the problem. It checks the edit against your goal, not just whether a crop was made.

column5: During a household-budget analysis, the user changes the rent amount in the shared spreadsheet. The agent recognizes the edit as a correction and updates its remaining-budget analysis using the new value.
column6: The agent is analyzing your household budget in a shared spreadsheet. You notice the rent figure is wrong and edit that cell yourself. The agent recognizes your edit as a correction, uses the new rent amount, and updates its remaining-budget analysis. You don't have to stop and explain the change in a separate message.

column5: While editing an image with a low vision user, the agent noticed that the user constantly use screen magnifier to read texts on the image editing app, so the agent suggests making the system font size larger.
column6: A low-vision user is editing an image and repeatedly moves a screen magnifier over small toolbar labels such as “Brightness” and “Contrast.” The agent recognizes this repeated action as a sign that the interface text may be difficult to read. It says, “I noticed you’re using the screen magnifier to read the editor labels. Would you like me to increase the system font size?” The agent offers the choices “Increase font size” and “Keep current size,” but makes no change until the user responds.

column4: Recognize when to involve the user
column5: An agent tidying a photo folder identifies files it proposes to delete. It presents the specific files and asks for approval before performing the deletion.
column6: You ask the agent to tidy a photo folder. It identifies files it thinks could be deleted, but doesn't remove them immediately. Instead, it presents the specific files and asks you to approve the deletion. It recognizes that this decision needs your involvement before it takes an action that removes your photos.

column4: Recognize when to involve the user
column5: A blind user asks the agent to share an album with a reading group. Before enabling link access, the agent explains the audience options and asks whether access should be restricted to named members.
column6: You ask the agent to share a photo album with your reading group. Before enabling link access, it explains who could open the album under the available sharing options. It asks whether access should be limited to named group members and waits for your choice before changing who can see your photos.

column4: Explain the work and next steps
column5: The user asks the agent what it's doing. The agent is preparing an expense report and explains that it extracted dates and totals from readable receipts, identifies two unreadable photos, and asks for clearer copies to finish.
column6: The agent is preparing your expense report, and you ask, ‘What are you doing?’ It replies, ‘I've extracted dates and totals from the receipts I can read. Two receipt photos are too blurry. I need clearer copies to finish.’ You learn what it's done, what's blocking it, and what needs to happen next.

column4: Explain the work and next steps
column5: A blind creator asks for missing on-screen cooking instructions to be added to a video’s audio description. The agent explains that it split a segment into shorter timed descriptions and is currently identifing where to review them.
column6: You're adding audio description to a cooking video and ask the agent to include instructions that appear only on screen. It explains, ‘I've split a segment into shorter descriptions timed to the video. I'm now finding the section for you to review.’ You can follow its work without having to inspect the video editor visually.

column5: A computer-use agent completes tasks by selecting, typing, using keyboard commands, navigating, and waiting when needed. It then reports progress through chat, audio, or visual annotations.
column6: The example shows a computer-use agent acting directly in interfaces. It can click or hover over controls, drag items, enter text, use keyboard shortcuts, scroll to relevant content, choose options, move between applications or documents, and wait for pages to load. After acting, the agent can provide feedback in three ways: a chat message, a spoken update, or a visual annotation placed directly on the interface.

column4: Provide help when the user is stuck
column5: A user repeatedly adjusts and undoes a photo crop. The agent notices signs of difficulty and offers help keeping the whole subject while removing empty space, waiting for the user’s response.
column6: You're cropping a photo, but keep adjusting the crop and undoing it. Without waiting for you to ask, the agent notices the repeated attempts and offers, ‘Would you like help keeping the whole subject while removing the empty space?’ It waits for your response, offering support without taking over your edit.

column4: Provide help when the user is stuck
column5: A blind user repeatedly restarts an attempt to select expense cells. The agent notices the repeated attempts and offers keyboard guidance without waiting for the user to ask.
column6: You're using a screen reader to select expense cells in a spreadsheet, but keep restarting the selection. The agent notices the repeated attempts. Before you ask for help, it offers, ‘Would you like keyboard guidance for selecting those cells?’ You can accept the support or keep working on your own.

column5: A user compares hotels on a laptop two days ago and then worked on something else, then opens the same saved assistant conversation tonight to keep working on hotel booking. The assistant continues with the two shortlisted hotels and the previously stated budget from the agent's memory.
column6: Two days ago, you compared hotels on your laptop, then moved on to other work. Tonight, you reopen the same saved conversation and say, ‘Let's continue booking a hotel.’ The assistant recalls the two hotels you shortlisted and the budget you gave it. You can pick up where you left off without repeating those details.

column5: A blind user used google map to explore the amphitheater in Balboa Park and were interested in stairs and entrance accessibility before traveling. The agent remembers her search history and when she's exploring Red Rocks Amphitheatre, the agent directly shows stairs and entrance accessibility info to the user
column6: Earlier, a low-vision user explored Balboa Park Amphitheater and focused on stairs and accessible entrances. Later, when the user opens Red Rocks Amphitheatre in a map app, the agent remembers those interests without requiring them to be repeated. It automatically adds accessibility information directly to the current map and venue photo, marking an accessible entrance, highlighting a step-free route from the parking area, and identifying a long stairway with handrails. This helps the user continue their accessibility research using relevant context from the earlier search.

column5: After researching pottery classes, a user asks the agent to keep the findings. The agent organizes dates, fees, and enrollment links in a memory page the user can return to.
column6: You've researched several pottery classes with the agent and say, ‘Keep these findings so I can come back to them.’ It organizes the class dates, fees, and enrollment links in a saved reference page. When you're ready to choose, the useful details are together instead of scattered through your earlier conversation.

column5: A blind student asks the agent to organize course-reading notes. The agent groups them under descriptive topic headings, retains source references, and saves a page the student can navigate with their screen reader.
column6: Your course-reading notes are becoming difficult to search through. You ask the agent to organize them for later study. It groups the notes under descriptive topic headings, keeps the source references, and saves them on a page you can navigate with your screen reader. You can return to a topic without rereading every note.
